subject: Can I perform scantwo permutation only in certain chromosomes?

messages.author: 49a67c6e0f03dace
messages.subject: Can I perform scantwo permutation only in certain chromosomes?
parts:
Hi Everybody!

I got a problem in performing scantwo permutation in my cross, because one chromosome has huge amount of markers and my results showed no QTL on that chromosome. So I'm thinking to perform the permutation of scantwo in the several chromosomes in which the significant QTLs are found.

But then I'm not sure whether the result is correct if I only run the permutation on some chromosomes, and my concerns are as followed:


(1) Penalties from permutations on several chromosomes are lower than the penalties from permutation on the whole genomes because of less marker number, which then results in more significant QTLs and interactions on the selected chromosomes.

(2) However, I do run the 1000-times permutation on the chromosomes that I want to test. So theoretically for the test on the selected chromosomes, the results are reliable?

I'm quite confused not. So could you please help me out?

Thanks a lot!!!!

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Can I perform scantwo permutation only in certain chromosomes?
parts:
There's not really any way to get around having to do the whole genome
two-dimensional scan, as the goal is to adjust for these multiple tests.

karl

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Can I perform scantwo permutation only in certain chromosomes?
parts:
Are you using calc.genoprob with step=0 so that calculations are performed only at the markers, or are you using step = some positive number, so that pseudomarkers get inserted?

I would assume that in the latter case, you've added more pseudomarkers so that the size of this intermediate object would be too large to be stored.

karl

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Can I perform scantwo permutation only in certain chromosomes?
parts:
You should increase the value of step. This argument indicates the distance between pseudomarkers and so the density of positions at which you are doing calculations. If the number of markers are different, presumably the chromosome lengths are somewhat different and so the number of markers and pseudomarkers you end up with will be different.

The appropriate value of step depends on the number of individuals and the type of cross, but I'm not aware of a case where you'd have mapping resolution to 0.001 cM, and seldom do you get precision < 1 cM, so I typically am using step=1 and occasionally like step=0.2. But step=0.2 usually in a targeted way, for example when I'm trying to get more precise endpoints for a LOD support interval.

karl

On 3/10/19 2:08 PM, ziming zhong wrote:
Yeah, I used calc.genoprob with step=0.001. But I used the same code for both populations. So I guess the number of pseudomarkers should be the same for both populations, if the marker number is the same?

Or shall I try to increase the step value?

On Sunday, March 10, 2019 at 7:42:00 PM UTC+1, Karl Broman wrote:
Are you using calc.genoprob with step=0 so that calculations are performed only at the markers, or are you using step = some positive number, so that pseudomarkers get inserted?

I would assume that in the latter case, you've added more pseudomarkers so that the size of this intermediate object would be too large to be stored.

karl

parts:
The plot of LOD score vs estimated recombination fraction for all marker pairs can reveal certain problems, like whether markers have their alleles switched. But it looks fine in your case. Marker pairs that are truly unlinked will have estimated rec frac that varies a bit +/- 0.5, with low LOD score, and that’s what you’re seeing.

To figure out marker order, I would first look at at plot of the pairwise rec fracs for a particular chromosome, or for pairs of chromosomes. (All chromosomes won’t be feasible given the large number of markers you have.) I’d then study large gaps in the estimated genetic map.

(Sometimes I accidentally reply to the individual rather than to the list; probably I did that in this case.)

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Can I perform scantwo permutation only in certain chromosomes?
parts:
I'm working on it now. The permutation finally works well after I change to step=2.5!

Thanks a lot Karl!!!!

On Monday, March 11, 2019 at 2:40:28 PM UTC+1, Karl Broman wrote:
The plot of LOD score vs estimated recombination fraction for all marker pairs can reveal certain problems, like whether markers have their alleles switched. But it looks fine in your case. Marker pairs that are truly unlinked will have estimated rec frac that varies a bit +/- 0.5, with low LOD score, and that’s what you’re seeing.

To figure out marker order, I would first look at at plot of the pairwise rec fracs for a particular chromosome, or for pairs of chromosomes. (All chromosomes won’t be feasible given the large number of markers you have.) I’d then study large gaps in the estimated genetic map.

(Sometimes I accidentally reply to the individual rather than to the list; probably I did that in this case.)

karl

On Mar 11, 2019, at 6:42 AM, ziming zhong <zm.zho...@gmail.com> wrote:

(Don't know why Karl's most recent reply is not shown here, but I stick his answer below.)

Thanks Karl! ok, I will try step=0.

About the map distance larger than 1000cM: I do have quite some markers with recombination fractions (rf) > 0.5, and i think those could be the reason why I got >1000cM in my genetic map. However, when checking the switched alleles with ‘checkAlleles(mydataChr01.cleanclean, threshold = 5)’, the results showed no apparent problems. Though rf > 0.5 indicates error, I also think there may not be problems with those markers, because those markers with rf >0.5 do not have large difference in LOD. Do I understand this result correctly? Should I delete those markers with rf > 0.5?

I attach the RF plot of this chromosome 1 here.

<Screen Shot 2019-03-11 at 12.18.33.png>





On 10 Mar 2019, at 20:59, Karl Broman wrote:

I would stick with step=0 if you have dense markers, and maybe use step=1 with stepwidth="max" if you have a few gaps. But you need to make it either 0 (no pseudomarkers) or a larger number like 2.5 or 5 if you're getting error messages about 'times value invalid' or running out of memory.

You want the step value in your permutations to match what you're using in the analysis.
And you want to finalize the genetic maps first. I don't think I've seen a chromosome with length 1000 cM.

karl

On Sunday, March 10, 2019 at 8:13:53 PM UTC+1, Karl Broman wrote:
You should increase the value of step. This argument indicates the distance between pseudomarkers and so the density of positions at which you are doing calculations. If the number of markers are different, presumably the chromosome lengths are somewhat different and so the number of markers and pseudomarkers you end up with will be different.

The appropriate value of step depends on the number of individuals and the type of cross, but I'm not aware of a case where you'd have mapping resolution to 0.001 cM, and seldom do you get precision < 1 cM, so I typically am using step=1 and occasionally like step=0.2. But step=0.2 usually in a targeted way, for example when I'm trying to get more precise endpoints for a LOD support interval.

karl

On 3/10/19 2:08 PM, ziming zhong wrote:
Yeah, I used calc.genoprob with step=0.001. But I used the same code for both populations. So I guess the number of pseudomarkers should be the same for both populations, if the marker number is the same?

Or shall I try to increase the step value?

On Sunday, March 10, 2019 at 7:42:00 PM UTC+1, Karl Broman wrote:
Are you using calc.genoprob with step=0 so that calculations are performed only at the markers, or are you using step = some positive number, so that pseudomarkers get inserted?

I would assume that in the latter case, you've added more pseudomarkers so that the size of this intermediate object would be too large to be stored.

karl

On 3/10/19 1:34 PM, ziming zhong wrote:
Hi Karl!

Sorry to bother you with the same problem again. There is something I don't really understand:

I have two cross populations with 250 individuals in each population. One population have 6000 markers and the scantwo permutation can be performed successfully. Another population have 4500 markers but the scantwo permutation always gave me the 'time' error as mentioned above.

I think it may not be the problem of too large number of markers, right? Could you give me some advice to solve the problem?

btw, in the error massage "rep(0, n.ind * n.pos * (n.pos - 1)/2 * n.gen^2)", I know n.ind means the number of individuals and n.pos means the number of markers. But I can't think out what does the n.gen stand for? 

Could you please help me out?


Thanks a lot!

On Monday, March 4, 2019 at 3:20:47 PM UTC+1, Karl Broman wrote:
It means with the number of markers you have, we can’t create an object large enough to do scantwo. 

karl

On Mar 4, 2019, at 7:50 AM, ziming zhong <zm.zho...@gmail.com> wrote:

Sorry Karl, I still have a question.

I keep getting this error massages:

Error in rep(0, n.ind * n.pos * (n.pos - 1)/2 * n.gen^2) : 
  invalid 'times' argument
Calls: scantwo ... scantwo.perm -> scantwo.perm.engine -> scantwo -> calc.pairprob
In addition: Warning messages:
1: In checkcovar(cross, pheno.col, addcovar, intcovar, perm.strata,  :
  Dropping 34 individuals with missing phenotypes.

2: In calc.pairprob(subset(cross, chr = thechr[i]), stp, oe, err, mf,  :
  NAs introduced by coercion

I kind of interpreted this error massage as that the amount of markers is too large, which causes the 'time' issue. Am I correct? Or is there a problem in my map?

Thanks a lot!!!



On Sunday, March 3, 2019 at 5:35:20 PM UTC+1, Karl Broman wrote:
There's not really any way to get around having to do the whole genome
two-dimensional scan, as the goal is to adjust for these multiple tests.

karl

On 3/3/19 4:14 AM, ziming zhong wrote:
> Hi Everybody!
>
> I got a problem in performing scantwo permutation in my cross, because
> one chromosome has huge amount of markers and my results showed no QTL
> on that chromosome. So I'm thinking to perform the permutation of
> scantwo in the several chromosomes in which the significant QTLs are
> found.
>
> But then I'm not sure whether the result is correct if I only run the
> permutation on some chromosomes, and my concerns are as followed:
>
>
> (1) Penalties from permutations on several chromosomes are lower than
> the penalties from permutation on the whole genomes because of less
> marker number, which then results in more significant QTLs and
> interactions on the selected chromosomes.
>
> (2) However, I do run the 1000-times permutation on the chromosomes
> that I want to test. So theoretically for the test on the selected
> chromosomes, the results are reliable?
>
> I'm quite confused not. So could you please help me out?
>
> Thanks a lot!!!!
